Newly hatched garfish larvae emerge from the chorion at a relatively advanced stage of development, a characteristic typical of belonid fishes. At the moment of eclosion, the standard body length of the prolarva measures 0.90 centimeters , while the total length from the tip of the snout to the end of the caudal fin extends to 0.978 centimeters . This initial size suggests a substantial yolk reserve that supports the endotrophic larva during the first days of life. When reared under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the embryos complete their development and hatch after a period of approximately 13.75 days , a relatively short incubation time that aligns with the rapid early ontogeny observed in many epipelagic teleosts. Upon emergence, these yolk-sac larvae remain largely inactive, relying on endogenous nutrients while their mouthparts and digestive systems continue to differentiate. The standard length at hatch of 0.90 centimeters  places Garfish larvae among the larger-bodied prolarvae within the Belonidae, an initial size that likely confers advantages in avoiding predation during the vulnerable transition to first exogenous feeding.

Following the initial yolk absorption phase, the larvae of Garfish undergo a rapid increase in body dimensions during the first few days after eclosion. By day one post-hatching, maintained at the same experimental temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the standard length has progressed to 0.95 centimeters , and the total length has reached 1.04 centimeters . This modest but consistent growth increment of approximately 0.05 centimeters in standard length over the initial 24-hour period reflects the efficient conversion of yolk reserves into somatic tissue. At three days after hatching, measured under identical thermal conditions of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the standard length has increased further to 1.305 centimeters , while the total length at this same age extends to 1.397 centimeters . The difference between the standard and total length measurements, which approximates 0.092 centimeters by day three, is attributable to the elongation of the caudal fin and the development of the characteristic beak-like jaws that begin to form during this early larval period. These data indicate a rapid early growth trajectory.

Sexual maturation in Garfish is tightly linked to the attainment of a specific body size, which shows a pronounced difference between the sexes. Females typically reach puberty when their total length measures 31.5 centimeters [Lp = 31.5 centimeters], a size that is noticeably larger than the 28.0 centimeters [Lp = 28.0 centimeters] recorded for males at the onset of gonadal maturation. This divergence in size at sexual maturity is a common pattern among iteroparous belonids, where the larger body size in females is thought to accommodate greater fecundity and larger egg production. The ultimate total length, representing the asymptotic size that individuals approach after many years of growth, also exhibits marked sexual dimorphism. Females attain a maximum total length of 93 centimeters [Li = 93 centimeters], whereas males reach a smaller upper size of 88 centimeters [Li = 88 centimeters]. This five-centimeter disparity in ultimate length is accompanied by a substantial difference in body mass, with the maximum recorded wet weight for females being 1300 grams [Wwi = 1300 grams], a figure that underscores the significant energetic investment required for reproductive output.

The lifespan of Garfish, determined from mark-recapture studies in the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean populations, indicates a maximum longevity of 7300 days [am = 7300 days] for individuals inhabiting waters with a mean annual temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This makes Garfish one of the longer-lived members of the Belonidae family, a group generally characterized by relatively short lifespans. The age at first reproduction, which typically follows the attainment of the size thresholds for puberty, is delayed compared to many other epipelagic teleosts. First spawning events have been recorded at an age of approximately 1095 days after hatching, which notably aligns with the size at puberty observed in females. The total length at puberty for females, previously noted as 31.5 centimeters, is reached when the fish have completed their juvenile phase and entered the sub-adult stage. The longevity of 7300 days [am = 7300 days] at 17 °C [T = 17 °C] allows for multiple spawning seasons, with females potentially producing several batches of eggs over their extended adult lives.

Ecologically, Garfish occupy a pelagic niche within coastal waters, where they are active predators of small schooling fishes and crustaceans. The thermal regime of their environment exerts a strong influence on their life history traits; for instance, the standard length at one day post-hatching of 0.95 centimeters  was recorded at a water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], a value that promotes rapid metabolic rates. Similarly, the total length of 1.04 centimeters  at one day and the standard length of 1.305 centimeters  at three days were both obtained under that same 22 °C [T = 22 °C] regime. In cooler waters, these growth rates would be substantially reduced, potentially delaying the onset of sexual maturation and extending the already considerable lifespan to beyond 7300 days [am = 7300 days] at a temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. The ultimate body mass of females, at 1300 grams [Wwi = 1300 grams], is a direct reflection of the food-rich coastal habitats they exploit, and this mass supports the high fecundity necessary for a species that produces pelagic eggs subject to high rates of natural mortality. The total length at puberty for males, 28.0 centimeters [Lp = 28.0 centimeters], indicates that males can begin reproducing at a younger age than females, a pattern that influences the operational sex ratio in spawning aggregations.
